newsitem.title: UK: British Steel sees over 1,500 job cuts 97/98.
newsitem.headline: British Steel sees over 1,500 job cuts 97/98.

text.p: British Steel Plc, which reported a collapse in year pre-tax profits to 451 million stg earlier on Monday, said it expected this year's job cuts to exceed the 1,500 losses seen in 1996/97.
Sir Brian Moffat, chairman and chief executive, declined to give an exact figure but told a press conference total job losses would be more than the job loss level seen in the last financial year.
British Steel also clarified it had made 61 million stg in provisions to pay for job loss costs in the period ahead.
Moffat said the speed and scale of the job cuts largely depended on how quickly British Steel could retrain staff to take on a wider range of skills.
In the future he envisaged all staff having the same employment terms. "The pace of job cuts this year compared to last year has already accelerated," he told the press conference.
"We are still negotiating with the unions on a plant by plant and year by year basis (on how many jobs will go). We want to put everyone on the same working conditions."
The job cuts are just part of a cost cutting drive introduced to grapple with the collapse in profitability stemming from the strength of sterling.

Moffat said the group also planned to clamp down on suppliers of raw materials and services. He saw a reduced number of suppliers in future and added that those suppliers who remain would have to meet tough new demands from British Steel.

"We're trimming our supplier base. We want from our suppliers zero (price) inflation and cost benefits on top of that." Moffat said British Steel wished to ask for the same exacting service it provided to its major customers -- the automotive industry.
The steel giant said cost cutting moves like these should help it make "significant" reductions to its cost base in an effort to maintain profitability.
On sterling's impact, the group said the combination of currency woes and sluggish steel prices in the last year had knocked around 400 million pounds off profits.
Last financial year, British Steel had accounted for an average sterling level of 2.46 Deutsche marks. Sterling has risen by around 20 percent since last summer against the German currency.
"We are not banking on it easing," said Moffat.
"We'd like the government to introduce fiscal policies alongside other measures as none of us wants inflation (growth). Fiscal policies would have a more direct impact," he added.
"We are determined, however, that although we can't control the exchange rate, our business will remain competitive."

On expansion and acquisitions, British Steel said its strong cash generation and non-debt position meant it was ideally placed to move on new deals. Moffat said the group would be prepared to increase gearing to 30 percent or higher if the right deal came along.
British Steel was not interested in buying western European steel companies but Moffat expressed interest in the Asia Pacific, China, and central and eastern Europe.
